searchText: <@301186049323958275> "Reference Implementation" implies an implementation that meets the spec so well that it can serve as a spec in it's own right. In the (I think common) case where the spec has been refined from one or more existing implementations none of them may meet the spec, but all may be useful as evidence that the facility being specified is useful, and to help reviewers to understand the spec. But yes, I bit more explanation than a bare link is appropriate. I would be fine if reference implementation is required to meet the spec strictly. What I really want is a way to reduce external links in EIPs. I think external links should live elsewhere, not in the specification. The spec for email addresses, doesn't contain a link out to where someone implemented an email parser, it either has an inline parser or none at all. I hear you, but it's a very good thing for specs to codify existing practice. For all but small proposals the implementations will be too large to be placed in the spec. > Hmm, apparently if you submit a PR that changes an EIP author, the bot will merge it if you are the *new* author? <https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/3040> <@!301186049323958275> it seems it only considers the current branch when checking authors and not `master`. The bot should extract authors from the EIP in `master`. I think this is not a terrible large change, I can give it a try later, but who knows how long will it take to get merged 🙂 Re: `Implementation` and other sections. No matter what is done, a lot of the sections/content remain as an opportunity for advertising and politics. If there is no implementation section, people can still refer to implementations in other sections, so not sure if this would solve the problem on its own. I generally don't think there is value in including links to external implementations, but that is the only pragmatic way to fill in that section. This has resulted in me telling basically everyone to just remove the section or inline their code. If they inline the code, then it is a reference implementation, which is why I thought renaming the section would help. I'd favour shrinking the number of sections. While I agree with the premise that people *can* always find places to include external links/advertisements, I think having a section named "External Links" *encourages* the behavior, and so we should avoid such sections. (as an extreme example) Implementations (note the plural) feels like it is begging for external links and advertisements. I wonder if we should have a `Use Cases` section though. How would this be different from `Motivation`? Make it explicit one needs to list actual use cases 🙂 My instinctual reaction is to not add even more sections that aren't "specification" (sections that are fuzzy/personal/political/etc.). However, I don't have a strong argument against that one at the moment. Maybe a sub-section of the Motivation? `Test Cases` and `Implementation` are the two ambiguous/not-well-used sections however. I do like Test Cases when someone actually includes them. For example, a hashing algorithm may have a list of preimages and hashes which is super useful to have in the EIP. However, you are correct that the section is rarely used. Even for those rare ones which have test cases listed, the actual testing suite is located elsewhere. I think the only two EIPs which have "reasonable" test cases listed are: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-145 and https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1052 Oh and https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2315 > I generally don't think there is value in including links to external implementations, but that is the only pragmatic way to fill in that section. ... If they inline the code, then it is a reference implementation, which is why I thought renaming the section would help. <@!301186049323958275> This is where I think we disagree. I see lots of value in implementations of a spec. Many implementations will be too large to inline, so references are the only way to include them. And being inlined is not what makes something a reference implementation. One tension seems to be that an EIP is both a proposed improvement and an argument for why it is an improvement, and such arguments may need to supporting external references. A general solution might be to pick a standard format for references in an EIP, including links, and clarify their appropriate use. > A general solution might be to pick a standard format for references in an EIP, including links, and clarify their appropriate use. <@!683653554631868440> this might be a useful step in any case, requiring properly formatted references instead of links makes it more likely that even in the case of a dead link the reference could be found. > an argument for why it is an improvement, and such arguments may need to supporting external references. <@!683653554631868440> Ah, I feel pretty strongly that EIPs **SHOULD NOT** be an argument, it should only be a technical spec. The argument for why should happen elsewhere. I *do* support a motivation section, but mainly just for historical purposes and it more or less just says, "here are some use cases and/or why this is a good thing" but not a formal argument. It's a matter of balance and taste, <@!301186049323958275>.

excerpts.author: gcolvin
excerpts.content:
> I generally don't think there is value in including links to external implementations, but that is the only pragmatic way to fill in that section.  ...  If they inline the code, then it is a reference implementation, which is why I thought renaming the section would help.
<@!301186049323958275> This is where I think we disagree.  I see lots of value in implementations of a spec.  Many implementations will be too large to inline, 
 so references are the only way to include them.   And being inlined is not what makes something a reference implementation.

One tension seems to be that an EIP is both a proposed improvement and an argument for why it is an improvement, and such arguments may need to supporting external references.   A general solution might be to pick a standard format for references in an EIP, including links, and clarify their appropriate use.
